common_name: Charissima Clematis (Rose-Pink Large-Flowered Clematis with Carmine Bar)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface and roots kept cool and shaded; Charissima flowers on the previous year's ripened wood in late spring and again lightly on new growth in late summer, so prune lightly after the first flush (Group 2).

directions: Raised by the Jackman nursery, Charissima bears large, rounded rose-pink flowers with a deeper carmine-pink bar down the center of each tepal and cream stamens. The main flush comes in late spring to early summer on last year's stems, with a lighter repeat flowering on new growth later in the season. As a Group 2 pruner it should only be lightly tidied in late winter, removing dead material and cutting live stems back to a strong bud, to preserve the earlier bloom.

common_name: Barbara Dibley Clematis (Mauve-Pink Large-Flowered Clematis with Carmine Bar)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface and roots shaded from direct sun; Barbara Dibley is an early large-flowered (Group 2) cultivar, so prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead wood rather than cutting hard.

directions: A long-grown Jackman introduction, Barbara Dibley produces very large mauve-pink flowers, each tepal marked with a deeper carmine-pink central bar that fades somewhat as the bloom ages. It flowers heavily in late spring to early summer on the previous season's stems, with a scattering of smaller blooms later on new growth. Give it a position with its flowers in sun but roots shaded and cool, and prune lightly as a Group 2 clematis to keep the framework of old wood that carries the big early flush.

common_name: Veronica's Choice Clematis (Double Pale Lavender-Blue Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface and roots cool and shaded; as a double early-flowering (Group 2) cultivar, prune only lightly in late winter so the previous season's wood that bears the double blooms is retained.

directions: Raised by Jim Fisk at his Suffolk clematis nursery, Veronica's Choice produces fully double, pale lavender-blue flowers packed with narrow tepals on the old wood in late spring and early summer, followed by simpler single flowers later in the season on new growth. The doubling is most reliable on mature, well-established plants in a cool-rooted, sunny position. Prune lightly as a Group 2 cultivar, removing only dead or weak stems, to keep the ripened wood that produces the showy double display.

common_name: Kathleen Dunford Clematis (Semi-Double Rich Pink Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface and roots kept cool and shaded; this early large-flowered (Group 2) cultivar should be pruned lightly in late winter rather than cut hard, to preserve the wood that carries the semi-double spring flush.

directions: A Jackman-raised cultivar, Kathleen Dunford bears richly colored, semi-double rosy-carmine-pink flowers with an extra ruff of inner tepals on the previous year's stems in late spring to early summer, followed by a lighter repeat of simpler single flowers on new growth. Like other early large-flowered clematis, it benefits from a cool, shaded root zone with its top growth reaching for the sun on a wall, obelisk, or fence. Prune lightly as a Group 2 cultivar, tidying dead growth and shortening stems to a strong bud rather than cutting the whole plant back hard.

common_name: Kacper Clematis (Purple-Blue Large-Flowered Clematis with Paler Bar)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface and roots cool and shaded; Kacper flowers over a long season on both old and new wood, so prune only lightly in late winter to remove dead or weak stems (Group 2).

directions: Bred by the Polish Franciscan friar and renowned clematis breeder Brother Stefan Franczak, Kacper carries large, wavy-edged purple-blue flowers with a slightly paler central bar on each tepal, in the tradition of his other well-known Warsaw-raised introductions. It blooms over a long season from late spring into late summer, flowering first on overwintered stems and then continuing on new growth. Grow it with its roots shaded and cool and its vines trained into full sun, and prune only lightly each late winter as a Group 2 cultivar to retain the older wood responsible for the earliest flowers.
